pos: n. (chance; fortune; that which happens without apparent design; luck)
etymology: Old Norse happ, chance, good luck. The word is the ancestor of happen, happy, and perhaps, though it stands alone in the Authorized Version as a single bare noun, naming the raw fact of an unplanned occurrence.
biblical_def:
Ruth's second chapter turns on this one small word at the exact moment the whole book pivots. Ruth, a Moabite widow gleaning to keep herself and Naomi alive, asks no favor and follows no plan beyond the ordinary law of gleaning; the text is careful to record that her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech. Nothing in the sentence claims Ruth aimed herself at that field, or that Boaz had summoned her there. By every visible measure it was chance, hap, an unplanned landing in one field among many she might have entered.

The rest of the book is Scripture's own commentary on that hap. Naomi, hearing where Ruth had gleaned, immediately recognizes what neither Ruth nor the narrative voice has yet said aloud — the man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen — and the whole redemption plot that follows, ending in the birth of Obed, the grandfather of David, unfolds from that one bare hap. The word is never explained away or spiritualized into a hidden miracle; it is left standing exactly as hap, an ordinary chance landing, and the book's quiet argument is that the LORD's providence works precisely through such unremarkable, undirected, entirely ordinary happenings, needing no more visible hand than a tired widow choosing one field over another.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): chance; fortune; that which happens or comes to pass without design; luck; hazard.
webster_full: HAP, n. That which happens or falls out; chance; fortune; luck; an event without apparent design.
GLEAN, v.i. To gather stalks or ears of grain left by reapers, as permitted to the poor under Mosaic law.
KINSMAN, n. A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
REDEEM, v.t. To buy back; to repurchase; to ransom; to recover a right or possession by payment or exchange.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; divine direction or superintendence.
scriptures: Rut 2:2
And Ruth the Moabitess said unto Naomi, Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn after him in whose sight I shall find grace. And she said unto her, Go, my daughter.
Rut 2:3
And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech.
Rut 2:20

And Naomi said unto her daughter in law, Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead. And Naomi said unto her, The man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen.
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Hap is treated as proof that no hand governs an outcome, when Ruth's whole plot is built to show that an event genuinely undirected by any visible human plan can still be entirely governed by the LORD's providence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; hap still names an unplanned occurrence. The principle worth recovering is how carefully the book of Ruth holds chance and providence together as one event seen at two heights, rather than erasing either to make the story simpler. Ruth's landing in Boaz's field really was hap, by every measure available to the people living through it; the text does not pretend she or anyone else steered it there.

Proverbs states the doctrine the narrative of Ruth only shows: the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD. A hap and a providence are not, in Scripture's own accounting, rival explanations competing for the same event — they are two true descriptions of the same event, seen from two different heights. What looked, from the ground, like an ordinary widow choosing one field among many looked, from the vantage the book itself supplies, like the exact hinge on which the ancestry of David and, in time, of Christ, would turn.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqreh (H4745), a happening, a chance occurrence; the noun behind “hap” in Ruth 2:3, from the verb qarah, to meet or befall.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqreh (H4745) — a happening, a chance, an accident; the noun rendered “hap” in Ruth 2:3.
Hebrew qarah (H7136) — to happen, to befall, to meet; the verb root behind miqreh, used of ordinary encounters throughout the Old Testament.
Hebrew laqat (H3950) — to glean, to gather up; Ruth's own activity at the moment her hap occurred.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; the office Boaz will come to fill because of this hap.
Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot; the object cast in Proverbs 16:33, the standing Old Testament figure for a matter left, on the surface, to chance.
usage: “her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz” — the small, unplanned turn on which the book of Ruth pivots.
“the man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen” — Naomi's recognition of what the hap had actually delivered.
“the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” — the doctrine underneath every such hap.

pos: a. (very large; of great bulk or extent; enormous)
etymology: Old French ahuge or ahoge, of uncertain further origin, possibly related to a root meaning fear or awe — a size great enough to inspire dread as much as measurement.
biblical_def:
The word appears once in the Authorized Version, inside the prophet Hanani's rebuke of King Asa. Asa, threatened by Baasha king of Israel, had hired the king of Syria with silver and gold from the temple treasury rather than trust the LORD, and Hanani's indictment reaches back to an earlier battle Asa had already won by faith to make its point: Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host, with very many chariots and horsemen? yet, because thou didst rely on the LORD, he delivered them into thine hand. The size of the enemy is not incidental to the rebuke; it is the whole engine of it. A huge host was no obstacle at all when Asa relied on the LORD, and no reminder of that fact should have been necessary a few years later against a far smaller threat.

Hanani's closing line supplies the doctrine the huge host was meant to teach: the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. A huge army, in this text, functions less as a threat than as a unit of measurement — the largest available scale against which to demonstrate that the LORD's strength is not proportioned to the size of the enemy at all, but to the wholeness of the heart that trusts Him. Asa had already been given the largest possible proof of that principle, which is exactly what made his later smaller failure of faith so much less excusable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): very great in bulk or size; enormous; immense; of unusual magnitude.
webster_full: HUGE, a. Very large; of great bulk, size, or extent; enormous; immense.
HOST, n. An army; a great multitude, especially one arrayed for battle.
RELY, v.i. To rest with confidence; to place trust or dependence upon, as upon a person or a promise.
DELIVER, v.t. To rescue; to set free; to release from danger, restraint, or the power of an enemy.
PERFECT, a. Complete; entire; wanting nothing essential; here, wholehearted or undivided in devotion.
scriptures: And at that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said unto him, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand.
Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host, with very many chariots and horsemen? yet, because thou didst rely on the LORD, he delivered them into thine hand.

For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars.

And Asa cried unto the LORD his God, and said, LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude. O LORD, thou art our God; let not man prevail against thee.
corruption_summary: The size of an obstacle is treated as the decisive factor in whether faith is reasonable, when Hanani's rebuke uses a huge, already-defeated host to prove the opposite: the LORD's strength is measured by the heart that trusts Him, not by the enemy's scale.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; huge still names sheer size. The principle worth recovering is the specific shape of Hanani's argument, which does not merely assert that God can handle big problems — it points to a documented case, Asa's own earlier victory, and asks why a demonstrated pattern was abandoned the moment a smaller test appeared.

Asa's prayer in chapter fourteen, before the huge host was even engaged, already contained the whole theology Hanani later has to remind him of: it is nothing with the LORD to help, whether with many or with them that have no power. The tragedy Hanani names in chapter sixteen is not that Asa failed to understand this principle in the abstract, but that he had already lived the huge-scale proof of it and let a smaller fear talk him out of the very confidence his own greatest victory should have made unshakeable.
roots_summary: Hebrew rob (H7230), abundance, multitude; the underlying idiom translated “a huge host” in 2 Chronicles 16:8, literally a host in abundance.
roots_lines: Hebrew rob (H7230) — abundance, multitude, greatness; the noun behind the idiom rendered “a huge host,” literally a host in abundance.
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — a host, an army, strength; the word for the host itself, paired with rob.
Hebrew sha'an (H8172) — to lean upon, to rely, to rest confidently; the verb behind “relied” both on Syria and on the LORD.
Hebrew shalem (H8003) — whole, complete, at peace; the word behind “perfect” describing the undivided heart the LORD seeks.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7200, causative of seeing) — to see, to look, run to and fro (H7751 shut is the actual verb of running); together, the LORD's eyes searching the whole earth.
usage: “Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host” — Hanani's reminder of Asa's earlier victory.
“because thou didst rely on the LORD, he delivered them into thine hand” — the outcome that huge host could not prevent.
“the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth” — the principle the huge host was meant to teach.

pos: n. (an irritating skin sensation causing a desire to scratch; a covenant curse named among the diseases of Deuteronomy)
etymology: Saxon giccan, to itch. The Authorized Version's one literal use names an actual skin affliction; its one figurative use, centuries later in English translation, borrows the same sensation for an appetite that cannot leave sound doctrine alone.
biblical_def:
Deuteronomy's covenant curses, spoken before Israel ever crossed the Jordan, include the itch among a short list of afflictions attached to covenant unfaithfulness: The LORD will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods, and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed. The itch here is named alongside diseases Israel had already seen firsthand in Egypt, redirected now as a possible covenant consequence rather than a plague inflicted on an enemy — the same LORD who once smote Egypt for Israel's sake could smite Israel herself if the covenant were broken, and this particular affliction is marked as one whereof thou canst not be healed, incurable by any human remedy.

Second Timothy borrows the same sensation for an entirely different but structurally similar condition: a time will come when men after their own lusts shall heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears, unable to endure sound doctrine and instead accumulating teachers who will scratch the specific itch their own lusts demand. The physical itch of Deuteronomy and the itching ears of Timothy share exactly the trait that makes the figure work: an itch does not resolve itself by being scratched, it only demands to be scratched again, and a congregation gathering teachers to match its own cravings is describing a condition, not a cure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an uneasy sensation in the skin, exciting a desire to scratch; a cutaneous disease attended by such sensation.
webster_full: ITCH, n. A cutaneous disease, marked by a troublesome sensation and eruption; also, an uneasy desire or craving.
BOTCH, n. A large ulcerous swelling; a boil; a plague sore.
SCAB, n. A crust formed over a healing sore; also, a disease of animals affecting the skin.
HEAL, v.t. To cure of a disease or wound; to restore to soundness.
SOUND, a. Free from defect, error or disease; whole; healthy; here, of doctrine, free from corruption or falsehood.
scriptures: But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:
The LORD will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods, and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.
corruption_summary: Itching ears are treated as simple curiosity or a taste for variety, when Paul names it a symptom of a specific inability to endure sound doctrine, matched by teachers gathered deliberately to feed the craving rather than to cure it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the physical word, but the figurative use in 2 Timothy names a temptation that has only grown more efficient with time: the deliberate cultivation of teachers who will say exactly what a listener's own lusts already wanted to hear, so that no doctrine ever has to be endured, only agreed with in advance.

Deuteronomy's itch is instructive precisely because it is named as incurable by human means — whereof thou canst not be healed — and the figurative itch of 2 Timothy carries the same structure. A congregation that heaps up teachers to match its cravings is not thereby satisfied; it has simply institutionalized the itch, guaranteeing a fresh supply of scratching and no possibility of the only real cure, sound doctrine received rather than curated.
roots_summary: Hebrew garab (H1618), an itch, a scab; one item in the covenant curse list of Deuteronomy 28:27; Greek knetho (G2833), to itch, to tickle, behind Paul's figure in 2 Timothy 4:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew garab (H1618) — the itch, a scab or eruption; the noun of Deuteronomy 28:27, listed among covenant-curse diseases.
Hebrew shechiyn (H7822) — a boil, a botch; the disease named first in the same verse, elsewhere the affliction of Job.
Greek knetho (G2833) — to itch, to tickle, to scratch; the participle behind “itching” in 2 Timothy 4:3, used only here in the New Testament.
Greek episoreuo (G2002) — to heap up, to accumulate; the verb behind “heap to themselves teachers.”
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy, whole; the standing New Testament word for sound doctrine, the very thing itching ears cannot endure.
usage: “the LORD will smite thee... with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed” — the covenant curse of Deuteronomy.
“having itching ears” — Paul's figure for a craving no true doctrine can satisfy.
“heap to themselves teachers... after their own lusts” — the deliberate feeding of that craving.

pos: a. (belonging to a person by birth; pertaining to the place of one's birth)
etymology: Latin nativus, from natus, born, the past participle of nasci, to be born. A native land is, at root, simply the land a man was born into, before any choice of his own entered the matter.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah's oracle against Shallum, the son of Josiah who reigned briefly as Jehoahaz before being carried captive to Egypt, gives the word its one appearance in the Authorized Version, and does so with unusual finality: Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country. The dead, meaning Josiah, is not the one to mourn; the living exile, carried off from the land of his birth with no promise of ever seeing it again, is the greater grief. Jeremiah reverses the natural instinct to weep hardest for the grave and directs it instead toward the harder fate of permanent exile from one's native ground.

The weight the prophecy places on never seeing one's native country again only makes sense against the whole Old Testament's assumption that the land itself was bound up with covenant identity — not merely a birthplace in the modern, sentimental sense, but the specific inheritance promised to the fathers. To be exiled forever from it was not simply homesickness; it was a living picture of covenant curse, the same threat rehearsed throughout Deuteronomy's warnings, now falling on one particular king by name. Shallum's native country was never his by mere accident of birth in Israel's own theology; it was covenant ground, and losing it forever was the specific and severe judgment Jeremiah is here commanded to announce.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): pertaining to the place or country of one's birth; also, born in a particular place or country.
webster_full: NATIVE, a. Belonging to one by birth; pertaining to the place or country where a person was born.
EXILE, n. Banishment; enforced removal from one's native country; also, the person so banished.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or promise, invoking God as a witness to the truth of what is declared.
INHERITANCE, n. That which is or may be inherited; a possession received by right of birth or covenant.
CAPTIVE, n. One taken prisoner, especially in war; one held in bondage or servitude.
scriptures: Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country.
For thus saith the LORD touching Shallum the son of Josiah king of Judah, which reigned instead of Josiah his father, which went forth out of this place; He shall not return thither any more:
By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
The LORD shall bring thee, and thy king which thou shalt set over thee, unto a nation which neither thou nor thy fathers have known; and there shalt thou serve other gods, wood and stone.
corruption_summary: Native land is flattened into a sentimental attachment to a birthplace, when Jeremiah's oracle and the covenant curses behind it treat exile from native ground as the visible enactment of a broken covenant, not homesickness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself; native still names what belongs to a person by birth. The principle worth recovering is why Jeremiah treats Shallum's permanent exile as a heavier grief than his father's death. In the Old Testament's own frame, the land of Israel was never merely a native country in the generic modern sense but a specific covenant inheritance, sworn to the fathers and held on the condition of obedience.

Psalm 137's weeping by the rivers of Babylon is the same grief given voice from the exiles' own side, and Deuteronomy's earlier curse names the mechanism behind it in advance: covenant unfaithfulness would end in exile to a nation Israel had never known. Shallum's lost native country is therefore not a private sorrow of displacement but a public, prophetic sign that the covenant curses were no longer merely threatened but had begun to fall.
roots_summary: Hebrew moledet (H4138), kindred, native land, birthplace; the noun behind “native country” in Jeremiah 22:10, from yalad, to bear or beget.
roots_lines: Hebrew moledet (H4138) — kindred, native land, birthplace; the word rendered “native country” in Jeremiah 22:10, the same used of Abraham's own homeland in Genesis 12:1.
Hebrew erets (H776) — land, earth, country; the general noun paired with moledet in this construction.
Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, to go into exile; the standing Old Testament verb for the captivity this oracle foretells.
Hebrew shuv (H7725) — to return, to turn back; explicitly and permanently denied Shallum, he shall return no more.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession; the covenant category the native land belonged to, deeper than mere birthplace.
usage: “he shall return no more, nor see his native country” — Jeremiah's oracle over Shallum's exile.
“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept” — the same exile's grief from within.
“The LORD shall bring thee... unto a nation which thou hast not known” — the covenant curse that made such exile possible.

pos: n. (the time of noon; midday, when the sun is at its highest and most exposing point)
etymology: A compound of noon, from Latin nona (hora), the ninth hour, and tide, an old word for time or season (as in Christmas-tide, Whitsuntide). Noontide is simply noon-time, the hour of fullest daylight, when nothing can any longer hide in shadow.
biblical_def:
The word's single appearance belongs to one of Jeremiah's bitterest personal laments, a curse pronounced not against Israel's enemies but against the very day of the prophet's own birth: let that man be as the cities which the LORD overthrew, and repented not: and let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide. The man cursed is the messenger who brought Jeremiah's father the news of his birth; Jeremiah wishes upon him, in his anguish, the full and inescapable horror reserved for cities like Sodom and Gomorrah, overthrown without repentance, their alarm sounding from morning's first light straight through to noontide's full glare.

Noontide's place in that curse is precise. Morning's cry could still, in principle, belong to a warning in time; a cry that continues unabated into noontide, the hour of greatest visibility and least possible concealment, describes catastrophe fully arrived and fully exposed, with no shadow left anywhere to hide the ruin from view. Jeremiah's lament sits inside a book otherwise devoted to calling a hardened nation to repent before such a noontide of judgment actually falls on them; that its most despairing chapter borrows the very hour of full disclosure to curse the prophet's own birth-day shows how completely Jeremiah, even at his lowest, understood exactly what an unrepentant noontide would mean.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): midday; the time when the sun is on the meridian; the middle of the day.
webster_full: NOONTIDE, n. Midday; the time of noon, when the sun has reached its highest point.
OVERTHROW, v.t. To overturn; to demolish; to bring to ruin, especially of a city or a kingdom.
REPENT, v.i. To feel sorrow or contrition for sin, with a purpose of amendment; to change one's mind for the better.
LAMENT, v.i. To mourn; to express deep sorrow, especially by outward signs, as weeping or wailing.
CURSE, n. A malediction; a solemn invocation of evil or injury upon a person.
scriptures: Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed.
And let that man be as the cities which the LORD overthrew, and repented not: and let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide;
Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven;
Jer 6:4
Prepare ye war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon. Woe unto us! for the day goeth away, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out.
corruption_summary: A prophet's raw lament of despair is either sanitized into mild poetic sorrow or read as evidence against the reliability of Scripture's own emotional honesty, when Jeremiah's cursing of his birth-day, noontide alarm and all, is preserved by Scripture precisely as the unedited cry of a real man carrying a call too heavy to bear without protest.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; noontide still names midday. The principle worth recovering is what it means that the book of Jeremiah preserves this lament at all, without softening it or explaining it away. A prophet whose whole ministry was announcing coming judgment on Judah, here wishes a form of that very judgment, cities overthrown without repentance, upon the day of his own birth.

Jeremiah 6:4's separate use of noon, an enemy army preparing to attack at the hour of greatest visibility, shows how consistently the prophet's imagination reaches for noontide as the hour nothing can escape unseen. That the same image turns, in chapter twenty, against Jeremiah's own birth-day is not a contradiction of his prophetic office but the clearest possible evidence of its cost: a true prophet's despair, honestly recorded, sits beside his faithfulness rather than disqualifying it.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsohorayim (H6672), noon, midday, the dual form suggesting the two halves of the day meeting; the noun behind “noontide” in Jeremiah 20:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsohorayim (H6672) — noon, midday; a dual noun, literally the two lights or two halves, the point where morning and afternoon meet.
Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to overturn, to overthrow; the standing verb of Sodom's destruction, applied here to the cursed man's imagined fate.
Hebrew nacham (H5162, negated) — to repent, to be sorry; explicitly denied of the overthrown cities, no repentance came before their ruin.
Hebrew arar (H779) — to curse; the verb opening Jeremiah's lament over his own birth-day.
Hebrew teru'ah (H8643) — a shout, an alarm, a battle-cry; the noun behind “shouting” heard from morning into noontide.
usage: “let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide” — Jeremiah's curse borrowing Sodom's own judgment.
“Cursed be the day wherein I was born” — the despair the noontide image serves.
“let us go up at noon” — the same hour used elsewhere of an army's open, undisguised approach.

pos: v.i. (to state an argument against; to raise a charge or accusation); n. (a thing presented to the mind or senses)
etymology: Latin objectus, past participle of objicere, to throw against, from ob-, against, and jacere, to throw. To object is, at root, to throw a charge against someone, setting an accusation in their path.
biblical_def:
The Authorized Version's one use of the word as a verb belongs to Paul's defense before Felix, and it appears in a sentence whose whole force depends on something conspicuously missing. Paul lists the Jews of Asia who had originally stirred up the temple crowd against him, and points out that they, of all people, are absent from this very trial where the actual accusation is being made: Who ought to have been here before thee, and object, if they had ought against me. The men best positioned to bring a real objection, having witnessed whatever supposedly happened, have not come; the charge is instead being pressed secondhand by others with no direct testimony to offer.

The verse works as a piece of careful legal argument, not merely a complaint. Paul does not simply deny the accusation; he names precisely who should have appeared to object, under Roman legal expectation, and lets their absence speak for itself. It is the same instinct Scripture elsewhere commends in Deuteronomy's law of witnesses, that no man should be condemned on hearsay where the actual accusers will not stand and object to his face. Paul's confidence before Felix rests not on rhetorical flourish but on the plain fact that no one qualified to object has been willing to do so under oath.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to oppose in words or arguments; to offer as a charge or ground of opposition; to bring forward as an accusation.
webster_full: OBJECT, v.i. To offer reasons or arguments against; to make a charge or accusation, especially before a tribunal.
ACCUSE, v.t. To charge with a crime or fault; to bring a formal accusation against.
WITNESS, n. One who testifies to a fact from personal knowledge; one who gives evidence in a legal proceeding.
TESTIMONY, n. Evidence given by a witness, under oath, concerning a matter of fact.
TRIBUNAL, n. A court of justice; the seat of a judge; a place where judgment is administered.
scriptures: Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me.
Who ought to have been here before thee, and object, if they had ought against me.

For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar.

One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
corruption_summary: An accusation is treated as credible simply for having been made loudly or repeatedly, when Paul's own defense turns on the specific, legally trained observation that the men who could actually object under oath have declined to appear at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word; to object still means to raise a stated charge against someone. The principle worth recovering is Paul's own discipline in constructing his defense: he does not merely assert his innocence, he identifies the specific procedural gap in the case against him, that the original accusers who stirred up the crowd in Asia are conspicuously not present to object in person.

Deuteronomy's law of witnesses supplies the standing biblical principle behind that discipline — no man condemned on the word of one witness, let alone on secondhand report from men unwilling to appear and object directly. Paul's confidence before both Felix and later before Festus, culminating in his appeal to Caesar, is not the confidence of a man daring the system to catch him, but of a man who has checked that the system's own rules of evidence have not actually been met against him.
roots_summary: Greek enkaleo (G1458), to call in, to accuse, to bring charges; the verb behind “object” in Acts 24:19, a legal term for lodging a formal complaint.
roots_lines: Greek enkaleo (G1458) — to call to account, to accuse, to bring a legal charge; the verb rendered “object” in Acts 24:19.
Greek kategoreo (G2723) — to accuse, to speak against; the more common verb used of Paul's accusers throughout Acts 24-25.
Greek apologeomai (G626) — to speak in one's own defense; the standing verb of Paul's own legal responses in this section.
Greek epikaleomai (G1941) — to call upon, to appeal; the verb behind Paul's appeal to Caesar in Acts 25:11.
Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; the office Deuteronomy 19:15 requires in plural before any charge can stand.
usage: “Who ought to have been here before thee, and object, if they had ought against me” — Paul's pointed observation of his accusers' absence.
“Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me” — the substance of Paul's defense.
“At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” — the law of evidence behind it.

pos: a. (remaining after an even number is subtracted; extra; not matching a set)
etymology: Old Norse oddi, a point of land, a triangle, hence a third or extra thing that does not pair evenly with another. An odd number is, at root, the number left standing alone once everything else has been paired off.
biblical_def:
Numbers' census of the Levites, taken by the month and upward rather than by the usual military age of twenty, produces a specific and awkward mismatch that the text handles with remarkable practical care. The firstborn of Israel numbered 22,273; the Levites numbered only 22,000, leaving the odd number of them — the 273 firstborn sons with no Levite substitute to redeem them by direct exchange — to be redeemed instead by a fixed payment of five shekels apiece, the money given to Aaron and his sons. The arithmetic did not come out even, and rather than round the number away or ignore the remainder, the law makes specific, individual provision for every single odd, unmatched firstborn son.

What the text quietly insists on is that an odd number, a remainder left over after the neat one-to-one substitution has been exhausted, is not a rounding error beneath the law's notice. Each of the 273 firstborn sons represented was a particular household's particular son, owed to the LORD by the same claim as every other firstborn in Israel, and the text will not let the census close until every one of them, down to the last odd man, has been accounted for and redeemed by name-equivalent payment. The God who counts a whole nation by tribe and family is shown, in this one administrative detail, also counting the leftover fraction that a less careful record might have simply dropped.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): not even; not exactly divisible by two; also, remaining over and above a certain number.
webster_full: ODD, a. Not even; that cannot be divided into two equal whole numbers; also, additional, over and above a stated round number.
REDEEM, v.t. To buy back; to ransom; to release from obligation or bondage by payment.
FIRSTBORN, n. The first offspring, especially of a family, holding a place of preeminence and, under the law, dedicated to the LORD.
SHEKEL, n. A Hebrew unit of weight and, later, of currency, used as the standard of the sanctuary.
SUBSTITUTE, n. One put in place of another; something used instead of another thing.
scriptures: Num 3:46
And for those that are to be redeemed of the two hundred and threescore and thirteen of the firstborn of the children of Israel, which are more than the Levites;
Num 3:47
Thou shalt even take five shekels apiece by the poll, after the shekel of the sanctuary shalt thou take them: (the shekel is twenty gerahs:)
Num 3:48
And thou shalt give the money, wherewith the odd number of them is to be redeemed, unto Aaron and to his sons.
Num 3:12
And I, behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn that openeth the matrix among the children of Israel: therefore the Levites shall be mine;
corruption_summary: A leftover remainder is treated as beneath careful accounting, a rounding error to be waved past, when Numbers three insists on redeeming every single odd, unmatched firstborn son by name-equivalent payment rather than letting the surplus simply go unaddressed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; odd still names what is left over after an even division. The principle worth recovering is the law's evident refusal to treat 273 individual firstborn sons as a statistical remainder rather than as 273 actual persons, each with a genuine claim on redemption that a tidier, rounder number would have satisfied automatically through the Levite substitution.

The five-shekel payment is not a discount or an approximation; it is a precise, individually calculated redemption price applied to precisely the number of people the neat substitution could not cover. A God who orders the substitution of an entire tribe for an entire category of firstborn sons, and then pauses to make sure the 273 who fall outside that clean exchange are not simply absorbed into the total, is shown counting in a way that leaves no odd remainder actually unaccounted for.
roots_summary: Hebrew adaph (H5736), to be over and above, to remain in excess; the verb behind “the odd number” in Numbers 3:48, describing an exact numerical surplus.
roots_lines: Hebrew adaph (H5736) — to be over, to remain in excess, to be a surplus; the root behind “the odd number of them” in Numbers 3:48.
Hebrew padah (H6299) — to redeem, to ransom, to buy back; the standing verb for the whole transaction this passage describes.
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — a firstborn; the category of person whose redemption the odd number concerns.
Hebrew sheqel (H8255) — a shekel, a unit of weight and money; the standard of payment fixed for each odd, unmatched firstborn.
Hebrew tachath (H8478) — instead of, in the place of; the preposition governing the whole logic of Levite-for-firstborn substitution in Numbers 3:12.
usage: “the odd number of them is to be redeemed” — the precise, individually accounted surplus of firstborn sons.
“five shekels apiece by the poll” — the fixed redemption price for each one.
“the Levites shall be mine” — the substitution the odd number fell outside of, and so required its own provision.

pos: n. (the act of persuading; a settled conviction or belief produced by argument or influence)
etymology: Latin persuasio, from persuadere, to persuade fully, from per-, thoroughly, and suadere, to advise or urge. A persuasion is a conviction that has been thoroughly worked into a man, whether by truth or by flattery.
biblical_def:
Paul's letter to the Galatians uses the word at the exact hinge of his argument against the false teachers who had persuaded a once-faithful church to add circumcision to the gospel of grace. Having asked Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?, he delivers a verdict on the persuasion itself, wherever its precise human source lay: This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you. The word here does not name error in the abstract; it names a specific, successful campaign of conviction that had genuinely taken hold in the Galatian churches, strong enough to turn them from a course they had begun well.

What makes Paul's verdict sharp is its indifference to how convincing the persuasion felt from the inside. He does not argue that the Galatians were stupid or that the false teachers were unpersuasive; he grants, if anything, that the persuasion had worked. His whole point is that a persuasion's actual origin, not its felt plausibility or its emotional force, is what determines its worth: this persuasion, however thoroughly it had been worked into them, did not come from the one who called them by grace, and its true source, not its psychological grip, is therefore what the Galatians must judge it by.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of persuading; the state of being persuaded; a settled opinion or conviction produced by argument or entreaty.
webster_full: PERSUASION, n. The act of influencing the mind by argument, entreaty, or reason; also, a fixed opinion or belief resulting from such influence.
HINDER, v.t. To obstruct; to impede; to prevent from progress or accomplishment.
GRACE, n. The free and unmerited favor of God; the divine influence operating in the heart for salvation.
GOSPEL, n. The good news of salvation through Jesus Christ; the doctrine of Christ's redemptive work.
CALL, v.t. To invite or summon; in theology, to invite effectually to salvation through the gospel.
scriptures: Gal 5:7
Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?
Gal 5:8
This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you.
Gal 1:6
I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: A persuasion's felt sincerity or emotional force is treated as evidence of its truth, when Paul's whole argument concedes the Galatians were genuinely, successfully persuaded and still condemns the persuasion outright on the basis of its actual source.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; persuasion still names a settled conviction produced by influence. The principle worth recovering is exactly what Paul's verdict refuses to grant: that a persuasion which has genuinely taken hold, changed real behavior, and felt entirely convincing from the inside might, for that very reason, be trustworthy.

Galatians one supplies the standard by which every persuasion, however effective, must actually be judged — not by its psychological grip but by whether it comes from him that calleth, the God of grace, or from another gospel dressed up convincingly enough to run alongside the true one. Paul's willingness to pronounce a curse on even an angel preaching a different gospel shows how completely the source, not the felt strength, of a persuasion determines its worth in his theology.
roots_summary: Greek peismone (G3988), a persuasion, a yielding to persuasion; the noun of Galatians 5:8, used only here in the New Testament, from peitho, to persuade.
roots_lines: Greek peismone (G3988) — a persuasion, a state of having been persuaded; a rare noun, used only at Galatians 5:8 in the whole New Testament.
Greek peitho (G3982) — to persuade, to win over, to convince; the verb root behind peismone.
Greek enkopto (G1465) — to hinder, to impede, literally to cut into a path; the verb behind “hinder” in Galatians 5:7.
Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call, to invite; the participle behind “him that calleth you,” the true source Paul contrasts with the false persuasion.
Greek anathema (G331) — a thing accursed, set apart for destruction; the fate Paul pronounces on any persuasion preaching another gospel, Galatians 1:8.
usage: “This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you” — Paul's verdict on the Galatians' false conviction.
“Ye did run well; who did hinder you” — the question the persuasion is measured against.
“so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ” — the true source that persuasion had displaced.

pos: n. (a place planted with trees or vines; the act of planting; a cultivated tract of ground)
etymology: Latin plantatio, from plantare, to plant. A plantation is, at root, simply the place where planting has been done and is being tended — the ground given over to deliberate cultivation rather than left wild.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel's riddle of the two great eagles and the vine, addressed to the house of Israel in the person of a rebellious king, uses the word for the tended ground a transplanted vine depends on. The first eagle, Babylon, took the top of a cedar and planted it as a low, spreading vine that turned its roots and branches toward its planter in complete dependence; then a second eagle appears, and the vine, already alive only because of the first eagle's care, foolishly bends toward the new one instead, hoping he might water it by the furrows of her plantation — seeking a second, unauthorized source of water for ground that already had a rightful keeper.

The riddle's interpretation, given later in the same chapter, names the vine as Zedekiah, planted and sustained by Nebuchadnezzar's authority yet secretly turning to Egypt for help, breaking the covenant sworn in the LORD's own name to Babylon. The plantation's furrows were never neutral ground available to whichever eagle could reach them first; they belonged to the one who had planted the vine there in the first place, under oath. A cultivated plantation, in Ezekiel's figure, is a picture of covenant obligation as much as agriculture — roots and furrows that owe their water, and their loyalty, to the one who planted them, and cannot honestly seek a second master without breaking faith with the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a place planted, especially with trees; a piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of crops; also, a colony newly settled.
webster_full: PLANTATION, n. A place planted, especially with trees or vines; ground appropriated to cultivation.
FURROW, n. A trench made by a plow; a channel cut in the ground for planting or irrigation.
VINE, n. A climbing or trailing plant, especially the grape-vine; often used figuratively of Israel.
COVENANT, n. A solemn agreement between parties, sealed by oath, obligating mutual faithfulness.
REBEL, v.i. To rise in opposition to lawful authority; to break allegiance or covenant obligation.
scriptures: Eze 17:6

And it grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and the roots thereof were under him: so it became a vine, and brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs.
Eze 17:7

There was also another great eagle with great wings and many feathers: and, behold, this vine did bend her roots toward him, and shot forth her branches toward him, that he might water it by the furrows of her plantation.
Eze 17:8
It was planted in a good soil by great waters, that it might bring forth branches, and that it might bear fruit, that it might be a goodly vine.

But he rebelled against him in sending his ambassadors into Egypt, that they might give him horses and much people. Shall he prosper? shall he escape that doeth such things? or shall he break the covenant, and be delivered?
corruption_summary: Seeking a second source of support is treated as prudent diversification, when Ezekiel's riddle judges the vine's turn toward a second eagle as covenant-breaking, precisely because the plantation's furrows already belonged, by oath, to the one who first planted it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a plantation still names cultivated, planted ground. The principle worth recovering is how completely Ezekiel's figure ties agricultural dependence to covenant fidelity. The vine's furrows are not open ground available to whichever eagle offers water; they are furrows already committed, by the vine's own planting and by Zedekiah's own sworn oath, to a single rightful source.

The riddle's blunt question in verse fifteen, shall he break the covenant, and shall he escape, refuses to treat the search for a second patron as harmless strategy. A plantation, in this text, is never a neutral resource to be leveraged toward whoever seems stronger at the moment; it is ground already bound by oath, and bending its roots toward a second eagle while still depending on the first is named, without euphemism, as rebellion against the very arrangement that kept the vine alive at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew matta' (H4302), a planting, a plantation; the noun behind “plantation” in Ezekiel 17:7, from nata', to plant.
roots_lines: Hebrew matta' (H4302) — a planting, a plantation; the noun rendered “plantation” in Ezekiel 17:7.
Hebrew nata' (H5193) — to plant; the verb root, used throughout the chapter of the vine's original setting.
Hebrew tela'ah (H8500, related to furrow imagery) or arug (H6170) — a furrow, a bed; the channel by which water reached the plantation.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the sworn obligation Zedekiah's turn toward Egypt is judged for breaking.
Hebrew marad (H4775) — to rebel, to revolt; the verb naming the vine's true offense in Ezekiel 17:15.
usage: “that he might water it by the furrows of her plantation” — the vine's disloyal turn toward a second eagle.
“It was planted in a good soil by great waters” — the original, rightful provision the plantation depended on.
“shall he break the covenant, and shall he escape?” — the riddle's verdict on that disloyalty.

pos: n. (the act of paying; the discharge of a debt or obligation by giving what is due)
etymology: Old French paiement, from payer, to pay, from Latin pacare, to pacify or satisfy, itself from pax, peace. A payment is, at its Latin root, whatever it takes to make a matter peaceable again between debtor and creditor.
biblical_def:
Christ's parable of the unmerciful servant turns entirely on a payment that cannot possibly be made. A servant owing ten thousand talents, an amount no ordinary laborer could repay across many lifetimes, stands before his king with no defense: forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made. The sentence is severe and, by the ordinary logic of debt, entirely just — a debt this size demands the only payment left available once money has run out, the debtor's own person and household sold to recover what can be recovered.

What makes the parable devastating is what happens next: the servant falls down and worships his lord, and the lord, moved with compassion, forgives him the whole debt outright, releasing him from a payment that was never actually going to be made even by the sale of everything he owned. Christ's whole point in the parable turns on what that same forgiven servant then does to a fellow servant who owes him a debt smaller by a factor of many thousands, refusing him the same mercy he had just been shown. Payment, in this parable, is not merely a financial transaction; it is the exact axis on which Christ measures whether a man who has received an impossible debt's forgiveness has understood anything at all about what he was given.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of paying; the discharge of a debt, or the fulfillment of an obligation, by giving money or its equivalent.
webster_full: PAYMENT, n. The act of paying; the discharge of an obligation by delivering money or its value.
TALENT, n. An ancient unit of weight and money, among the largest in Scripture, representing great value.
DEBT, n. That which is owed by one person to another; an obligation to pay or perform.
COMPASSION, n. A feeling of sorrow or pity for the sufferings of another, moving one to relieve them.
FORGIVE, v.t. To pardon; to give up resentment or claim for compensation; to remit a debt or offense.
scriptures: Therefore is the kingdom of heaven likened unto a certain king, which would take account of his servants.
And when he had begun to reckon, one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents.
But forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.
Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt.
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is treated as the automatic erasure of a debt too small to matter, when Christ's parable is built entirely on a debt so large that payment was structurally impossible, making the king's forgiveness costly rather than casual.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; payment still means the discharge of a debt. The principle worth recovering is the deliberate scale Christ builds into the parable. Ten thousand talents was not a debt a servant could plausibly have accumulated through ordinary means, and the payment commanded, the sale of his wife, children, and all he had, would not have come close to satisfying it either — the debt was, by design, beyond any payment the servant himself could ever supply.

The forgiven servant's subsequent refusal to extend even a fraction of that same mercy to a debtor who owed him a comparatively trivial sum is what exposes the whole point of the parable: a man who has genuinely understood what it cost to have an impossible payment cancelled cannot turn around and demand a payable one from someone else without revealing that he never understood the gift at all. Christ's warning that follows, of the unmerciful servant delivered to the tormentors, ties the doctrine of forgiveness directly to whether a forgiven debtor forgives in turn.
roots_summary: Greek apodidomi (G591), to give back, to pay off, to render what is due; the verb behind “to pay” and “payment” throughout the parable of Matthew 18.
roots_lines: Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, to pay off, to render fully; the verb underlying both “to pay” and “payment” in Matthew 18:25-28.
Greek talanton (G5007) — a talent, the largest unit of currency in the New Testament, used here to signal a debt beyond ordinary repayment.
Greek opheilo (G3784) — to owe, to be indebted; the standing verb for the servant's obligation.
Greek splagchnizomai (G4697) — to be moved with compassion, literally in the bowels; the king's response that cancels the payment altogether.
Greek aphiemi (G863) — to send away, to forgive, to release from obligation; the verb behind “forgave him the debt” in Matthew 18:27.
usage: “he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold... and payment to be made” — the debt's demanded, impossible price.
“moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt” — the payment cancelled outright.
“one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents” — the scale that makes the forgiveness costly, not casual.
